content.text: Build your app once, deploy that same artifact to every environment, and give it its settings when it starts. A separate build per environment means production runs an artifact nobody tested, and it bakes URLs, and sometimes secrets, into the image. Keep in the build only what's the same everywhere; everything that varies between deploys belongs in the environment.

QA signs off on staging on Tuesday. On Wednesday, the release job checks out the same commit, builds it again with the production settings, and deploys. Checkout breaks in production, and staging can't reproduce it. The production image was built a day later than the one QA tested, and something under it had changed in between. Two builds of one commit, and production got the one nobody tested.
The common misconception

The belief: each environment (dev, staging, production) needs its own build, with its settings baked in. Staging gets a staging build, production gets a production build, and each one is complete and ready to run.
Smart developers believe this because their tools teach it. Angular's docs describe file replacements, "an option for substituting source files before executing a build", and say that combined with
--configuration
this "provides a mechanism for configuring environment-specific data in your application." To add staging, the same page has you copy
environment.ts
to
environment.staging.ts
and add a staging build configuration. If the official way to set an API URL is a build flag, a build per environment looks like the design.
The half-truth: the app does need to know where it runs. It can learn that when it starts, though, and that's the only way to deploy exactly what you tested.
What actually happens
Build, release and run are separate stages

The Twelve-Factor App splits a deploy into three stages. The build stage turns the code into "an executable bundle known as a build." The release stage "takes the build produced by the build stage and combines it with the deploy's current config." The run stage starts it. Config joins at release, after the build is finished, so one
build artifact
can become many releases: one for staging, one for production. And "Every release should always have a unique release ID", so you can always tell which build and which config are running.
A second build is a second artifact
Two builds of the same commit aren't guaranteed to be identical. The earlier articles showed why: a base image tag can move between builds, and a cached
RUN

step can hold different packages on different machines. Even with every input pinned, a per-environment build differs on purpose, because the settings are part of it. In our run, the staging and production images got different image IDs, so the image you tested is not the image you ship. A
deployment pipeline
gets its confidence from promoting the same artifact through each stage.
Config is what varies between deploys

The Twelve-Factor definition is precise: config is "everything that is likely to vary between deploys (staging, production, developer environments, etc)", such as database handles, credentials and hostnames. Routes or how modules are wired together don't count, since that kind of setting "does not vary between deploys, and so is best done in the code." Its litmus test is worth running on your repo: could you publish the code "at any moment, without compromising any credentials"?
Values baked into an image travel with it

Docker's docs warn that "Build arguments and environment variables are inappropriate for passing secrets to your build, because they're exposed in the final image." That's true of every build-time value: anyone who can pull the image can read it. In our test,
docker history
printed the production URL twice, once from
ENV
and once from the
ARG
itself.
The fix: one image, config at startup
Both tabs build the same
server.ts
(below) on Docker 29.4.3 with
node:24.22.2-alpine3.24
. The wrong one bakes the URL in with a build argument:

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
# Dockerfile: ARG PAYMENTS_URL, then ENV PAYMENTS_URL=$PAYMENTS_URL
docker build --build-arg PAYMENTS_URL=https://sandbox.payments.example \
  -t shop-api:1.4.0-staging .
docker build --build-arg PAYMENTS_URL=https://api.payments.example \
  -t shop-api:1.4.0-prod .
docker image ls --format '{{.Tag}} {{.ID}}' shop-api
# 1.4.0-prod e6cf6bf4ae98
# 1.4.0-staging 5911098ae226
docker history --format '{{.CreatedBy}}' shop-api:1.4.0-prod | grep PAYMENTS
# ENV PAYMENTS_URL=https://api.payments.example
# ARG PAYMENTS_URL=https://api.payments.example

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
docker build -t shop-api:1.4.0 .
docker run -d --name shop-staging \
  -e PAYMENTS_URL=https://sandbox.payments.example shop-api:1.4.0
docker run -d --name shop-prod \
  -e PAYMENTS_URL=https://api.payments.example shop-api:1.4.0
docker logs shop-prod
# shop-api 1.4.0, payments at https://api.payments.example
docker inspect --format '{{.Name}} {{.Image}}' shop-staging shop-prod
# /shop-staging sha256:c6339bd7a8c12e3a83c260e9b2357033791d8896232c273dab406b7eebc1c7f6
# /shop-prod sha256:c6339bd7a8c12e3a83c260e9b2357033791d8896232c273dab406b7eebc1c7f6

content.text: The app reads its config once, at startup, and refuses to start without it:

In the first tab, one commit became two images with two IDs, and the production URL is readable by anyone with the image. In the second, both containers run the image with the same ID, and only the variable differs. Starting it with no
PAYMENTS_URL
exits right away with
Error: PAYMENTS_URL is not set
, which is far better than failing on the first payment.

rows.text: Given to the container at run time

blocks.title: In ASP.NET Core, environment variables already win

content.text: WebApplication.CreateBuilder
reads environment variables after
appsettings.json
and
appsettings.{ENVIRONMENT}.json
, so they override both. For nested keys, the docs note that a double underscore "is automatically converted into a colon":
Payments__BaseUrl
sets
Payments:BaseUrl
. The environment's settings file is chosen when the app starts, so it's still one build.

blocks.title: Frontend bundles are built with their values inside

content.text: A browser can't read your server's environment variables, which is why Angular swaps its environment files in at build time. To build a single-page app once, have it fetch a small
config.json
at startup that each environment serves. Keep secrets out of both: Angular's docs warn that environment files are bundled into the app and "visible to anyone who loads the page", and a fetched
config.json
is just as public.
How to apply it in your project
Go through your build scripts, Dockerfiles and pipeline for per-environment values: URLs, hostnames, credentials, feature switches. Each one is config.

items.title: Move it out of the build

content.text: Replace build arguments, compile-time defines and file replacements with values read at startup, and fail fast when one is missing.
Build once per commit, tag it with the version or commit SHA, record its digest, and deploy that digest to staging and then production. The latest-tag article showed why the digest matters.

items.title: Give secrets to the container, not the image

content.text: Pass credentials at run time from your platform's secret store, never as build arguments, and check
docker history
on your current images for anything that leaked.
Key takeaways

items.text: Build once; config joins at release, so one artifact can run in every environment.
A per-environment build means production runs an image that was never tested.
Config is whatever varies between deploys; read it at startup and fail fast when it's missing.
values stay in the image, so never use them for secrets.
Promote the same digest from staging to production, and roll back by redeploying the previous one.
